discriminating_test: The finding has two separable parts. (A) OBSERVATION: numeric /do/card/NNNNNN URLs exist on the www host (not only on m.), and they are duplicates of the www slug URL for the SAME card on the SAME host. The discriminating test is not "does a www numeric URL appear in a site: probe" (the previous evidence) — that only re-observes the symptom and is contaminated by the search API loosely honoring path-scoped site: operators. The real test is: take a specific www numeric URL, read its indexed title, then search that exact title independently and see whether a www SLUG URL for the same card also exists in the index. If both www forms appear with the same title, same-host duplication is established and the /do/card/ route on www is proven not to be folded into the slug URL. fix_assessment:
The direction (301 the www numeric alias to the www slug, rather than adding a cross-canonical) is sound, and 301 rather than canonical is the right call for reclaiming links. Three cautions.

1. BIGGEST RISK — the fix explicitly says "Keep m./do/card/{id} as-is; that one ... needs the alternate/canonical pairing in the next finding." If the m. card page's rel=canonical currently points at the www NUMERIC URL (very plausible, since the numeric ID is the form the two hosts share, and it is the only www URL the mobile template can build without a slug lookup), then 301ing www/do/card/{id} makes every mobile canonical target a redirect, converting ~the entire mobile card corpus into canonical-to-redirect chains. Google usually follows that to the slug, but it is signal loss and a well-known source of canonical churn. These two findings must therefore ship together, or the m. canonical must be repointed at the slug URL FIRST and the www 301 shipped second. Shipping the www 301 alone is the dangerous ordering.

2. "This is a one-line route change ... the ID→slug mapping already exists, since both render the same card" is an inference, not a verified fact. Rendering the same card only proves the route resolves an ID to a card record; it does not prove the record stores, or the router can construct, the canonical slug path (category/subcategory/nameNN.html). If it cannot, this is a data/backfill job across the card table, not a one-liner, and the effort rating "small" is optimistic.

3. Deindexation risk is low — 301 consolidates rather than removes, and the slug form is already indexed. But the two degenerate-title numeric URLs (330206, 101633) hint that some numeric views may not map cleanly to a slug page; those need a defined fallback (410 or redirect to the category) rather than a 301 to a slug that may not exist, or the route change will emit redirect loops or 404s at scale.

fix_assessment:
Step 2 (self-canonical on /p/n>1, no canonical to page 1) is sound and matches current Google guidance since rel=prev/next was retired. Two real collateral-damage risks in the rest:
(1) Step 1 puts rel=canonical AND meta robots noindex on the same /s/<fmt> page. These are contradictory signals, and the documented risk is that consolidation propagates the noindex to the canonical target — i.e. the unfaceted /do/cards/<subcat> category pages, the ones actually worth ranking, can themselves drop out. Pick one per URL: noindex,follow on the facet views (preferred, since it also cuts the pagination combinations) or canonical, not both. I could not fetch developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/consolidate-duplicate-urls to quote this — it is egress-blocked here — so treat the mechanism as from memory and confirm against that page before shipping.
(2) Step 3's `Disallow: /do/cards/*/s/` is riskier than the finding's sequencing caveat admits. Even shipped after the noindex is processed, a permanent disallow means Googlebot can never re-read those pages, so they can linger as URL-only index entries, and the "follow" in noindex,follow dies the moment the path is blocked. If deep cards (page 4 through 8 of a facet view) are discoverable mainly via these listings, blocking the path orphans exactly the money pages the finding wants to protect. Safer: keep noindex,follow permanently and skip step 3, or ship a card-level XML sitemap first so discovery does not depend on the facet crawl paths.

fix_assessment:
Directionally right, and path parity is confirmed, but the preferred fix as written has one real operational hazard and one SEO trap.
HAZARD: the finding itself notes h-source "appears to be an origin/source box behind the CDN". A blanket path-for-path 301 to www would, if the CDN pulls from this box, bounce the CDN's own origin fetches back to the public www hostname — a redirect loop or an origin outage for the live site. The rule must be keyed on the incoming Host header (redirect only when Host is h-source.123g.us / any *.123g.us, pass through when Host is www.123greetings.com as a CDN origin pull sends it), never on path alone. Get that wrong and you take the site down, not just the mirror.
SEO TRAP: do not implement this via robots.txt Disallow on the mirror. A robots-blocked URL cannot be recrawled, so Google never sees the 301 or the noindex and the mirror URLs linger as URL-only entries. The order is: serve the 301 (or X-Robots-Tag: noindex), leave the host crawlable until the mirror URLs drop out, then lock it down. Option (b) — IP-allowlist/HTTP auth — is correct as the end state but must come AFTER the redirects have been crawled, otherwise the indexed mirror URLs 403 and consolidate nothing.
SCOPE: apply to m-source.123g.us and m-src.dev.123g.us too, not just h-source; the dev host is arguably the more embarrassing one to leave public.
COLLATERAL DAMAGE RISK OTHERWISE: low. These are duplicate-host URLs consolidating onto live www equivalents; no unique content is lost, and no www ranking depends on the mirror.

fix_assessment:
The diagnosis is right but the fix as written is dangerous and should not be shipped unmodified. Three problems.

(1) COLLATERAL DAMAGE — the blanket `*.123g.us` rule is the serious one. The fix treats the whole zone as dev, but the evidence splits it: dev.123g.us and its children (www.dev, m-src.dev, webqc.dev) are unambiguously non-production, whereas h-source.123g.us and m-source.123g.us read as live ORIGIN hosts ("h-source" = html source, "m-source" = mobile source) that production delivery may pull from. Putting basic auth or an IP allowlist in front of those, or stamping `X-Robots-Tag: noindex` at the LB for any Host matching `*.123g.us`, could break production content delivery or — if any production URL resolves through those origins — deindex production pages. Split the rule: lock down `*.dev.123g.us` immediately, and investigate what depends on `*-source.123g.us` before touching it.

(2) SELF-DEFEATING SEQUENCE — the fix stacks `X-Robots-Tag: noindex` AND a robots.txt disallow on the same hosts. A robots.txt Disallow blocks the crawl that is required for Google to SEE the noindex, so the URLs stay indexed as bare references indefinitely. Order matters: serve noindex, let it be crawled and the URLs drop out, and only then disallow (if ever). Likewise, basic auth "makes noindex unnecessary" is true going forward but does not clear URLs already in the index — a 401 on an indexed URL deindexes slowly.

(3) GSC removals are temporary (~6 months) and require verifying each host as its own property, which the fix's "once connected" parenthetical glosses over. They are a stopgap for the visible entries, not a remedy.

The "audit DNS for the full *.123g.us zone" instruction is well-judged and my probe supports it empirically: I found a fifth host the auditor missed using search alone, which is direct evidence that search-based enumeration is incomplete and a zone transfer / DNS audit will surface more.

fix_assessment:
Mostly sound, with three real problems.

1. MATERIAL GAP — the facet instruction does nothing. "Create m/sitemap.xml ... explicitly exclude /s/<format> and /p/<n> URLs" treats sitemap exclusion as a crawl control. It is not. Sitemaps only add discovery; omitting a URL never discourages crawling or removes it from the index. The /s/ and /p/ URLs I confirmed indexed will keep being crawled from internal links regardless. Suppressing them requires robots.txt disallow, noindex, or rel=canonical to the unfaceted hub — none of which this fix contains. Shipping this fix as written and expecting the crawl trap to close would be a silent failure.

2. REAL COLLATERAL RISK — the m. sitemap. Publishing a sitemap that submits m. URLs as first-class entries is off-guidance for separate-mobile-site setups and risks pushing Google to treat m. URLs as independent indexable documents rather than alternates of www. If the rel=canonical / rel=alternate pairing is anything less than perfect (unverifiable here — host blocked), that is a duplicate-content and canonical-split risk on the entire card corpus, i.e. it could make things worse. Safer sequencing: verify the alternate/canonical annotations first, and only add an m. sitemap if that audit shows discovery genuinely failing.

3. MINOR — sitemap-profiles.xml. Actively submitting a UGC profile class (which /profile/all/ suggests is large) invites quality evaluation of pages that may be thin. Gate on the same thin-page filter proposed for tags.

The rest is correct and low-risk: the sitemap-index structure, the 50,000-URL child cap, and especially "if that column does not exist, omit the lastmod element entirely rather than synthesizing one" — that last point is exactly right and is directly backed by Google's stated position that lastmod must correspond to reality or trust in it is withdrawn for the whole site. No deindexation risk from the www-side changes.

fix_assessment: Three real risks. (1) HONESTY OF VideoObject: Google requires VideoObject to be on "a page where users can watch the video" and forbids marking up content not present on the page; violations are quality-guideline breaches that can be "marked as spam". 123Greetings cards are a mix of true video and GIF/animated-canvas ecards. Applying this template blanket-wide across the card template would stamp VideoObject onto every animated-but-not-video card — trading one unsupportable type (Product) for another, with manual-action exposure. Gate the template on "this card has a real video file" and fall back to CreativeWork/ImageObject otherwise. (2) THE TEMPLATE'S OWN EXAMPLE FAILS THE DURATION FLOOR: the fix writes `"duration": "{{ISO8601_DURATION e.g. PT28S}}"`. Google's video documentation states a 30-second minimum total duration; a 28-second exemplar tells the template author the wrong thing, and typical ecard runtimes sit right at that boundary, so much of the corpus may be video-ineligible regardless. (3) INVENTED ENDPOINT: `"embedUrl": "https://www.123greetings.com/embed/card/{{CARD_ID}}"` is a URL pattern the finding assumes rather than observed. If no such endpoint exists, every card emits an embedUrl that 404s — an invalid required property on every page, worse than the status quo. Verify or drop it and rely on contentUrl. Also: removing Product markup is defensible on its own merits, but the expected payoff is rich-result eligibility, not rank recovery — framing this as fixing the May 14 cliff sets up a false expectation and could push the team to ship a wide template change and then attribute unrelated core-update recovery to it. NORMATIVE — type list. Google's own doc (title indexed as "Review Snippet (Review, AggregateRating) Structured Data | Google Search Central") is corroborated by independent summaries: "Google currently supports review snippets for types including Product, Book, Recipe, Movie, Event, SoftwareApplication, and Course, while LocalBusiness and Organization are restricted to sites that capture reviews about other businesses or organizations rather than reviews about themselves"; "Google allows review or aggregateRating structured data for a specific list of item types, and these are the only content types currently eligible for review snippets in Google Search"; "Reviews for Organization, Place, or Person are not eligible for display as rich results." VideoObject, ImageObject and CreativeWork appear nowhere on any reproduction of that list. VideoObject was found only in its separate capacity as the video-rich-result type ("required properties including name, description, thumbnailUrl, and uploadDate"), i.e. a different feature, not review snippets. The finding's list (Book, Course, Event, LocalBusiness, Movie, Product, Recipe, SoftwareApplication) matches.
NORMATIVE — count properties. "AggregateRating requires itemReviewed, ratingValue, and either ratingCount or reviewCount... ratingCount or reviewCount (one is required)." And on the semantic distinction the finding asserts: "If you only collect ratings on your website, using ratingCount likely makes more sense"; "If you allow people to post reviews... it is more common to use reviewCount"; "the reviewCount property provides Google with a count of how many aggregated reviews are on a page. This data is independent of how many ratings were provided"; and crucially "Google seems to display ratingCount as 'votes', while reviewCount as 'reviews'." So the finding is right that both pass validation (the failure is silent, not an error) and right that they are not synonyms.
NORMATIVE — visibility/match. "Review content must be readily available to users from the marked-up page, and it must be immediately obvious to users that the page has review content"; "The aggregateRating and reviewCount in your schema must exactly match the numbers visible on your page — if your code says '100 reviews' but your page says '95 reviews,' that's a violation"; "a small implementation mistake such as marking up reviews that aren't visible, using an unsupported schema type, reporting an outdated review count, or adding self-serving reviews incorrectly can make your markup ineligible for a rich result." Note the documented consequence is INELIGIBILITY, not a ranking penalty. Self-serving enforcement is scoped to LocalBusiness/Organization since 2019.
CAUSAL — rival tested. The May 2026 core update "began rolling out globally on May 21, 2026, and was completed on June 2, 2026" (start 8:40 AM PDT May 21), with third-party peak volatility on the weekends of May 23 and May 30. A cliff dated May 14 PREDATES that rollout by a week, so the core update does not explain a May 14 breakpoint. PREMISE — no evidence either way. Nothing I could reach shows what the card template actually emits.
corrected_claim:
CONFIRMED as written: aggregateRating must not be ported onto VideoObject or ImageObject. Those types are not on Google's closed review-snippet eligibility list, so an aggregateRating attached to them will not produce stars. Also confirmed: ratingValue plus at least one of ratingCount/reviewCount is required, both pass validation identically (so the Rich Results Test stays green either way and the failure is silent), the two properties are not synonyms, ratingCount is the semantically correct property for a page that collects star votes rather than written reviews, and Google requires the marked-up figures to be visible to users and to match what the page displays. The recommendation to delete aggregateRating rather than re-home it is sound on the documentation alone.
NOT SUPPORTED, three corrections. (1) "Since the comments block is JS-injected, that count is very likely not present in rendered HTML at all, which breaks Google's rule" — this conflates server-rendering with visibility. Googlebot renders JavaScript; the documented requirement is that review content be readily available to users on the page and that the figures match, which JS-injected content can satisfy. Restate as: the figure must be visible to users and must match the marked-up integer; whether it is server-rendered is a crawl-reliability concern, not a stated policy violation. (2) "An unsupported-type signal at worst" — no source states that aggregateRating on an ineligible type is a negative signal. The documented outcome is that the markup is ignored / ineligible. Restate as: inert markup, nothing worse. (3) "Prior work already traced the May 14 ranking cliff to the Product/review-snippet dual-typing" — this is an inherited causal attribution I could not test. I did eliminate the most obvious rival (the May 2026 core update began May 21, not May 14), which is mildly favourable to the finding, but elimination of one rival is not attribution. Restate as: a May 14 breakpoint is not explained by the May 2026 core update; the schema cause remains unverified pending GSC.
Finally, the whole finding is premised on the card template currently containing Product + aggregateRating with reviewCount. I could not observe that premise at all. If the template does not contain aggregateRating, the finding is moot rather than wrong.
fix_assessment:
The core action — delete aggregateRating rather than re-home it onto VideoObject/ImageObject — is sound and low-risk, and correctly characterised as markup-only with zero UX change. The renaming guidance (reviewCount to ratingCount wherever aggregateRating is retained, with the integer matching a server-rendered visible figure) is correct and worth doing.
Three collateral risks the fix does not flag. (1) REAL STAR LOSS. If the card pages are currently earning star rich results from Product + aggregateRating, removing them removes the stars and the CTR they carry. The finding argues this is necessary and permanent, which follows from the type list, but it should be stated as a deliberate, irreversible CTR cost to be measured, not as a free cleanup. Any recovery hypothesis must clear that hurdle. (2) THE SIBLING CHANGE IS THE RISKIER ONE. The fix ships VideoObject/ImageObject in the same atomic release. VideoObject has its own required properties and represents an actual video; if the greeting cards are animations rather than real video files with a contentUrl/embedUrl, thumbnailUrl and uploadDate, then swapping Product for VideoObject substitutes one misrepresentation for another and is itself exposed to a structured-data manual action. That risk is larger than the aggregateRating removal and is unexamined. (3) ATTRIBUTION. Bundling three changes into one atomic release is defensible for avoiding a third broken state, but it guarantees that if the canary recovers you cannot tell which of the three did it — and the finding simultaneously relies on an unverified attribution of the original cliff. Step 4 (verify www and m. in Search Console before shipping) is the single most valuable item in the fix and should be a hard gate, not a step. Step 5 (stars only on a genuinely purchasable page with its own Product node) is correct and consistent with the documentation.

discriminating_test: The finding bundles an observation (deep /p/<n> URLs are indexed carrying the homepage title string) with a root cause (out-of-range page numbers return 200 OK with EMPTY results, making /p/<n> an unbounded soft-404 crawl trap). Two separate tests. (a) OBSERVATION: site: probes of the index for the four named URLs, checking each one's indexed title verbatim — the index is the right instrument here, since a title tag is exactly what it records. (b) CAUSE: the generic title only evidences "out-of-range + empty results" if that string appears ONLY where pagination runs past the last page. The discriminating check is therefore to look for the same generic string on a URL that is NOT out-of-range pagination, and for the correct hub title on a deep /p/<n> page. Either one breaks the inferred cause and replaces it with the rival explanation: a site-wide default/fallback title emitted by the m. template whenever the page-specific title fails to populate, for whatever reason. Settling emptiness itself needs the response body, which is unreachable.
test_run: Six WebSearch site: probes against the live index (all 123greetings/123g.us hosts are egress-blocked, so no fetch was attempted; one WebFetch to html.duckduckgo.com for result SNIPPETS — which would have shown whether the deep pages' bodies are empty — returned EGRESS_BLOCKED, so no body text was obtainable from any source). Probes run: site:m.123greetings.com/do/cards/birth_wishes; site:m.123greetings.com inurl:/p/; site:m.123greetings.com "Free Greeting cards, Wishes, Ecards, Birthday Wishes, Funny Cards & Gifs"; site:m.123greetings.com/do/cards/birth_wishes/s/videos; site:www.123greetings.com free greeting cards ecards; site:m.123greetings.com viewecard.
evidence_found:
OBSERVATION — all four named URLs reproduced verbatim from the index, exactly as the finding states:
- https://m.123greetings.com/do/cards/birth_wishes/p/12 → title "Free Greeting cards, Wishes, Ecards, Birthday Wishes, Funny Cards & Gifs | 123 Greetings"
- https://m.123greetings.com/do/cards/birth_wishes/s/videos/p/14 → same generic string
- https://m.123greetings.com/do/cards/birth_wishes/s/videos/p/4 → "Birthday Wishes & Messages Cards, Free Birthday Wishes & Messages Wishes | 123 Greetings" (correct hub title)
- https://www.123greetings.com/ → "Free Greeting cards, Wishes, Ecards, Birthday Wishes, Funny Cards & Gifs | 123 Greetings" — so the generic string IS the homepage title tag, as claimed.
CAUSE — two pieces of counter-evidence found in the same probes:
1. https://m.123greetings.com/do/viewecard is indexed with that identical generic string, and viewecard is a FUNCTIONAL page (the ecard-retrieval form: "click the link sent to your email, or type your ecard number in the search box"), not a paginated listing and not out-of-range. The finding itself notes this URL but treats it as corroboration; it is the opposite — it shows the string appears where no pagination exists, so the string cannot by itself evidence "page number exceeded the last page" or "empty results".
2. https://m.123greetings.com/do/cards/insp_sympathy/s/videos/p/11 is indexed with its CORRECT hub title ("Inspirational Sympathy & Condolences Cards, Free Inspirational Sympathy & Condolences Wishes | 123 Greetings"). Page 11 of a sympathy VIDEO facet is at least as likely to be out of range as page 12 of birth_wishes — the site's largest birthday sub-category — yet it renders the proper title. Depth does not switch the title, and no evidence establishes that /p/12 exceeds birth_wishes' last real page; the finding assumed it.
PREVALENCE — the inurl:/p/ probe returned 10 paginated m. URLs; the deepest page numbers seen anywhere were 14, 12, 11, 5, 5, 3, 2, 2, 1. Nothing resembling an unbounded integer space appeared. site:www.123greetings.com inurl:"/p/" returned no www URLs at all in this pattern, so the finding's "the identical space on www" is untested. A ~10-result US-only API cannot establish counts either way.
corrected_claim: CONFIRMED as stated: m.123greetings.com serves the www homepage's exact title tag ("Free Greeting cards, Wishes, Ecards, Birthday Wishes, Funny Cards & Gifs | 123 Greetings") on at least three indexed URLs — /do/cards/birth_wishes/p/12, /do/cards/birth_wishes/s/videos/p/14 and /do/viewecard — while sibling pages in the same category and facet (/s/videos/p/4) carry their correct hub title. This is a real duplicate-title / template-fallback defect and it is in Google's index. NOT SUPPORTED: that the trigger is pagination depth or out-of-range page numbers, that those pages return empty result sets, that the /p/<n> space is unbounded, or that this is where crawl budget is going. The pattern fits a simpler rival the evidence actively favours — the m. host emits a site-wide DEFAULT title whenever the page-specific title fails to populate, on at least one non-paginated URL type (/do/viewecard) as well as on some deep listing pages, with the failure condition unidentified. One indexed page at depth 11 (insp_sympathy/s/videos/p/11) carries the correct title, which is incompatible with a clean "past the last page → generic title" rule. Whether the affected pages are empty is unknown: no response body was obtainable from any reachable source.
fix_assessment:
Two of the three prescriptions carry real collateral-damage risk, and the one safe part is not the one the finding leads with.
1. "Return 404 when the requested page exceeds the last page with results" — correct practice in the abstract, but the finding never established that any named URL IS out of range. birth_wishes is the site's largest birthday sub-category and page 12 may well hold real cards; shipping a 404 rule derived from this evidence risks deindexing live inventory listings. Gate it on an actual count check in the controller, never on "the title looked generic".
2. "Add robots.txt Disallow for the /s/ facet dimension" — directly harmful on this evidence. /do/cards/birth_wishes/s/videos/p/4, /birth_milestone/s/postcards/p/1, /birth_fun/s/videos/p/2, /gen_sorry/s/videos/p/, /insp_sympathy/s/videos/p/11 are all indexed with correct, distinct, category-specific titles — these are working facet hubs, not junk. Disallowing /s/ would strip them from the index over time and lose whatever format-intent rankings they hold. Worse, Disallow blocks crawling but not indexing: URLs already known stay indexed as bare, snippet-less entries, so it would not even clean the pages the finding is worried about, and it would block Googlebot from ever seeing the corrected titles or canonicals shipped by fix 1. If a facet genuinely must go, noindex (crawlable) is the instrument, not Disallow.
3. The genuinely safe, cheap fix the finding under-weights: make the m. template never fall back to the homepage title — give every route, including /do/viewecard, a unique title, and add self-referential canonicals to paginated pages. Zero deindexation risk, and it fixes the one thing actually proven here.
blocking_gap: Two of the three open questions need one HTTP request each against an egress-blocked host. (a) Status code and body-emptiness: `curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://m.123greetings.com/do/cards/birth_wishes/p/12` and the same for /s/videos/p/14, then `curl -sS https://m.123greetings.com/do/cards/birth_wishes/p/12 | grep -c 'do/card/'` to count card links in the body — zero card links plus 200 confirms the soft-404; a non-zero count refutes the "empty results" claim outright and leaves only the title bug. (b) Where the range actually ends: walk `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{size_download}\n' https://m.123greetings.com/do/cards/birth_wishes/p/$n` for n in 1..20 and find the page where the card count drops to zero; if that boundary is below 12, the finding's cause is reinstated, and if birth_wishes paginates past 12 it is dead. (c) Unboundedness, the crawl-trap premise: same one-liner at n=500 and n=99999 — 200 with a rendered shell at n=99999 proves the infinite space, 404 disproves it. None of this is obtainable here: every 123greetings.com and 123g.us host returns EGRESS_BLOCKED, archive.org is blocked, and html.duckduckgo.com — the one route to third-party SERP snippets that might have shown body text — is blocked too, which is why emptiness could not be probed even indirectly. Google Search Console's Crawl Stats and the "Crawled - currently not indexed" / "Duplicate without user-selected canonical" reports on this property would settle prevalence and the crawl-budget claim, which no external tool available here can.

discriminating_test: The finding bundles three separable claims, each with its own test. (A) THE CORE MEASUREMENT — "a non-JS crawler sees ~30 words on a card page, because the card media is injected by Load_Video_Card into an empty div and comments/tabs are JS-loaded." The only test that separates this from the rival explanations (page has server-rendered prose but Google chooses a short meta-description snippet; or content is server-rendered but visually below the fold) is to diff the raw HTTP response body against the rendered DOM: `curl -sA "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Googlebot/2.1)" https://www.123greetings.com/birthday/happy_birthday/birthday191.html | sed -e 's/<[^>]*>/ /g' | wc -w` and grep the same body for `Load_Video_Card`. Snippet length in a SERP is NOT that test — Google prefers the meta description regardless of body length, so a short snippet is consistent with both a 30-word page and a 900-word page. (B) THE FIX'S PREMISE — "blog.123greetings.com already hosts a large, well-templated corpus at exactly these slugs." Test: site: probe of the index for the nine named slugs. (C) THE DOWNSTREAM INFERENCE — "Google cannot disambiguate the ~500 near-identically-titled cards in a subcategory." Test: site:123greetings.com/birthday/happy_birthday and inspect indexed titles for per-card differentiation.
test_run: Test A: attempted and BLOCKED. `curl -sS -m 25 -A "Googlebot/2.1" https://www.123greetings.com/birthday/happy_birthday/birthday191.html` returned `curl: (56) CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403` (HTTP:000, BYTES:0); same for blog.123greetings.com. Test B: ran `site:blog.123greetings.com birthday messages what to write in a card`. Test C: ran `site:123greetings.com/birthday/happy_birthday`, plus the exact-phrase probe `123greetings "teddy bear" birthday card "birthday hug to your dear ones"`, plus two negative probes: `site:123greetings.com "what to write in a" birthday card message examples` and `what to write in a birthday card for grandma 123greetings`. Also attempted to verify the scaled-content policy language at developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies — EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the policy caution below is flagged as unverified-here, not cited.

NOT FOUND / NOT TESTABLE: nothing confirming the "~30 words" count, nothing confirming `Load_Video_Card` or the empty-div mechanism, nothing distinguishing raw HTML from rendered DOM.
corrected_claim: Card-detail pages under /birthday/happy_birthday/ carry, at minimum, a one-sentence descriptive line (13-17 words, verified for birthday141) and near-boilerplate titles that differ only by a short card name — with at least two sampled cards having no card-specific title at all — while blog.123greetings.com already hosts a large, well-templated, message-rich corpus at exactly the slugs the finding names (verified: /what-to-write-in-a-card/, /birthday-messages/, /birthday-messages-for-grandpa/, /birthday-messages-for-grandma/, /birthday-messages-for-across-the-miles/, /invitation-messages/), and no card-detail page surfaces for "what to write" message queries. The specific figure "~30 crawlable words" and the stated ROOT CAUSE — that the shortfall is a JS-rendering artifact (Load_Video_Card injecting into an empty div, comments and Latest/Related tabs client-loaded) rather than simply a page that was never written to contain body copy — are UNVERIFIED here; both require the raw HTTP body, which is unreachable. The distinction matters for two downstream claims: (i) Googlebot does execute JavaScript, so if the content is merely JS-deferred it may still be indexed for Google, and the "cannot rank / cannot disambiguate" argument holds much more strongly for non-rendering LLM/AEO crawlers than for Google; (ii) if instead the body copy simply does not exist in any form, the JS framing in the fix ("server-render it") is beside the point and the real work is authoring/joining content. The prescription is sound either way; the mechanism attribution is not established.
fix_assessment: The fix's premise is verified — the source text genuinely exists on the blog — and the finding already anticipates the biggest hazard (seeded distinct subsets per card rather than verbatim syndication at scale). Remaining risks worth stating: (1) SELF-CANNIBALIZATION. The blog posts are themselves ranking assets (blog.123greetings.com/birthday-messages-for-grandma/ surfaced for the plain query "what to write in a birthday card for grandma"). Pushing the same messages onto 30,000 card pages can cause the card pages to compete with, and outrank-then-underperform, the blog post that currently earns the click. Excerpt 5-8 examples with a prominent link to the full post, rather than reproducing the list, and measure the blog post's own traffic as a guardrail metric, not just the card pages'. (2) SCALED-CONTENT-ABUSE EXPOSURE. Generating a near-identical block across ~30,000 URLs from a small mapping table is the shape Google's spam policies target; I could not fetch developers.google.com to quote the current wording (EGRESS_BLOCKED), so treat this as a flag to verify before rollout, not a citation. The seeded-subset design plus a genuinely per-subcategory heading mitigates it; a single shared block across all birthday cards would not. (3) SUBDOMAIN SPLIT. Cross-linking to blog.123greetings.com does not consolidate authority onto www; if the strategic goal is card pages that rank, consider whether the blog should live at www/... rather than building 30,000 outbound links to a separate host. (4) The "ship on happy_birthday first and measure" staging is the right call and should be treated as mandatory, not optional, precisely because the root cause is unverified — if the deficit turns out not to be JS-related, a server-rendering change alone will move nothing and the pilot will reveal that cheaply. (5) Minor: inserting a block "below the card and above the ads" shifts ad position and can affect layout stability and revenue; get that measured alongside the SEO metric. No deindexation risk identified.
blocking_gap: Raw HTTP body of a card page, which no available tool can reach (both www.123greetings.com and the sibling www.123cards.com return EGRESS_BLOCKED / proxy 403). The one-line test that settles it, run from an unblocked machine: `curl -sA "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Googlebot/2.1; +http://www.google.com/bot.html)" https://www.123greetings.com/birthday/happy_birthday/birthday191.html > raw.html; sed -e 's/<script[^>]*>.*</script>//g' -e 's/<[^>]*>/ /g' raw.html | tr -s " \n" " " | wc -w; grep -c "Load_Video_Card" raw.html`. That yields the crawlable word count and confirms or kills the JS mechanism in one shot. To separate "thin in raw HTML" from "thin even after rendering" (the Googlebot-vs-LLM-crawler distinction), pair it with the URL Inspection tool in Search Console for the same URL, or https://search.google.com/test/rich-results?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.123greetings.com%2Fbirthday%2Fhappy_birthday%2Fbirthday191.html and read the rendered HTML tab. For prevalence — which no tool here can establish — a Screaming Frog crawl of /birthday/ with JavaScript rendering disabled, exporting the Word Count column, would give the distribution across the ~500-per-subcategory and ~30,000-page claims.

fix_assessment:

The strategy is sound but the spec contains one concrete deindexation/ranking risk and one avoidable inconsistency, both of which I would change before shipping.

1. REAL COLLATERAL-DAMAGE RISK — item 1 of the split spec says to build /what-to-write-in-a-birthday-card/ and "consolidate with existing /birthday-messages/ via 301, do not run both". I confirmed /birthday-messages/ is live and indexed with a strong title ("500+ Birthday Messages — Heartfelt, Funny & Unique Wishes") and a fresh update signal, and it is the head of a working spoke cluster whose children all link on the `-messages` convention. 301-ing an established, indexed head page onto a brand-new URL to gain a keyword-string match in the slug is a bad trade: it forfeits the URL's accumulated history and internal-link graph, incurs re-crawl and re-evaluation lag, and creates redirect hops from every existing birthday spoke. 2. NAMING INCONSISTENCY — the blog's established, working convention is `<occasion>-messages` (/birthday-messages/, /invitation-messages/, /anniversary-messages-for-dad/, /birthday-messages-for-uncle/). 4. SEQUENCING — items 2–7 (sympathy, retirement, wedding, graduation, get-well, new-baby) are pure additive builds against a verified gap, carry no redirect and no cannibalisation risk, and can ship immediately without waiting on the hub question. CLAIM 1 — group non-merging: CONFIRMED, and it is the subtler of the two rules, stated correctly by the finding. Google's "How Google Interprets the robots.txt Specification" (developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/robots_txt, also served at developers.google.com/crawling/docs/robots-txt/robots-txt-spec): "Google's crawlers determine the correct group of rules by finding in the robots.txt file the group with the most specific user agent that matches the crawler's user agent. Other groups are ignored." And: "a user agent can match only one rule set, which is the first, most specific group that matches a given user agent." The combining behaviour that does exist is narrower and does not rescue the `*` group — Google: "If there's more than one specific group declared for a user agent, all the rules from the groups applicable to the specific user agent are combined internally into a single group"; RFC 9309 (datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9309): "If there is more than one group matching the user-agent, the matching groups' rules MUST be combined into one group." That is merging of several groups naming the SAME agent, not merging of `*` into a named group. So the finding's operative warning — add `User-agent: GPTBot` and GPTBot stops reading the `*` group, therefore every Disallow must be repeated inside each named group — is correct as stated, and the pasted file does in fact repeat its Disallow block in sections 1, 3 and 6.

CLAIM 2 — Google-Extended: CONFIRMED verbatim from Google's own documentation: "Google-Extended does not affect a site's inclusion in Search, nor is it used as a ranking signal in Search," and sites use it to control "whether their content helps train future versions of Gemini models." The "it fetches nothing / is not a crawler" characterisation is corroborated by the Google Search Central thread titled "Google-Extended does not visit the site" (support.google.com/webmasters/thread/355910235).

CLAIM 3 — Anthropic: CONFIRMED verbatim from the primary source, support.claude.com/en/articles/8896518, fetched in full. IP verification endpoint confirmed as https://claude.com/crawling/bots.json. Every element of the finding's Anthropic paragraph, including the paraphrased quotation, checks out against the page.

CLAIM 4 — Bing/Copilot: CONFIRMED. Microsoft documentation states Bing and Copilot "rely on the same core crawling, indexing, and ranking foundation as traditional search," and that for Bing-powered features "for example, grounding in Copilot or Bing Custom Search — only pages that are public and indexed by Bing can be used." fix_assessment:
The pasted file is technically well-formed and its policy reasoning is sound — it correctly repeats Disallow blocks inside each named group (the trap it warns about), correctly separates citation crawlers from training crawlers, and correctly declines to add Crawl-delay. But the delivery instruction is unsafe as written, and this is real collateral-damage risk, not a style objection.

1. BLIND WHOLESALE REPLACEMENT. The instruction is "Paste at https://www.123greetings.com/robots.txt" — overwriting a file that nobody in this audit has read. Any existing Disallow lines protecting crawl-budget sinks, faceted/parameter URLs, internal search results, staging paths or genuinely sensitive endpoints are silently deleted, because the replacement's `*` group only carries the six Disallows the auditor guessed at. On a site of this size an unknown existing exclusion set is very likely non-empty. The file must be read first and merged, never replaced.

2. THE m. HOST MIRROR IS THE SHARPEST RISK. "Mirror to m.123greetings.com" pushes an allow-all posture onto a mobile host whose current crawl policy is unknown. Separate m-dot hosts are very commonly disallowed or canonicalised away precisely to suppress a full duplicate of the desktop site. Opening it up and advertising a sitemap for it could induce large-scale duplicate-content indexation — the inverse of the intended benefit, and slow to unwind.

3. UNVERIFIED SITEMAP URLS. Both `Sitemap:` lines are asserted, not confirmed to exist. Shipping a robots.txt that advertises two 404s is a self-inflicted crawl error in Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools.

4. MINOR, FAILS OPEN. The `Disallow: /do/cards/*/p/` style wildcards are a Google/Bing extension, not part of RFC 9309. PerplexityBot, CCBot and other simpler parsers may treat the `*` literally and ignore the rule. Harmless direction of failure (those paths get crawled rather than wrongly blocked), but the file should not be described as portable.

5. The three closing rules (no global Crawl-delay; verify UAs via published IP JSON before WAF-blocking; robots.txt cannot stop non-compliant fleets) are correct and are the most immediately actionable part of the finding.

Correct sequencing: retrieve all three live files, diff against this template, merge additively, then deploy and validate in Search Console's robots.txt report and Bing Webmaster Tools.

GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User and ClaudeBot extract text from the initial HTML response only; ClaudeBot downloads JS in ~23.84% of requests and never runs it. This is unchanged as of Q2 2026. Googlebot (and Gemini via Google's infrastructure) is the exception, so a page can rank on Google while being empty to answer engines."

(b) SITE-SPECIFIC PREMISE — asserted, not verified here: "123greetings card pages server-render roughly 30 words; the card media, message, comments and Related/Latest tabs are JS-injected." Everything downstream — the ~30-word chunk losing retrieval comparisons, and the Product+VideoObject JSON-LD being unverifiable against a media-free DOM — is *conditional on (b)* and inherits its unverified status. The finding currently states (b) as established fact; it should be marked "observed once in an earlier session, not re-tested" until someone runs the curl. Separately, the claim generalises from what reads as a single card template to the whole card corpus; that generalisation is plausible for generator-produced pages but is not itself evidenced, and nothing available here (US-only WebSearch, ~10 results, no counts) can establish prevalence.
fix_assessment:
The fix's direction is right and its acceptance test is exactly the discriminating test — that part is well designed. Three concrete problems: 1. EFFORT IS UNDERSTATED, and the finding contradicts itself on the hardest item. Item (2) asks for "the card's printed message/verse as literal text in a

" while the finding elsewhere says that text is "currently locked inside a video file." If the verse is rendered into the video artwork, no template change extracts it — it needs transcription or re-authoring per card across the whole corpus. That is not a "generator-template change" and not "medium" effort. Items (1), (4) and (5) — poster , comments, Related/Latest as real — genuinely are template changes and should be split out and shipped first; they are cheap, safe, and independently valuable. 2. SCALED-CONTENT RISK on item (3). "80-150 words of server-rendered descriptive copy per card" across a corpus this size will in practice be template-generated or LLM-generated. Mass-produced near-duplicate descriptive copy is precisely what Google's scaled content abuse policy targets, so a fix aimed at answer engines could draw a spam action on the Google traffic that currently works — the one channel the finding concedes is healthy. Mitigation: derive copy from genuinely per-card facts (artist, occasion, format, duration, actual depiction) and accept shorter, or roll out to a sample and monitor before scaling. 3. UGC EXPOSURE on item (4). Rendering the top 5-10 user comments into crawlable HTML on every card page exposes unmoderated third-party text at scale; it needs spam/abuse filtering and a quality floor, and comment blocks should not be the bulk of the page's indexable text. Low collateral risk: no deindexation hazard. Adding server-rendered content and real anchors does not remove anything Googlebot already sees post-render, so items (1), (4), (5) are close to strictly additive. Do NOT let this fix remove the JS enhancement path — the finding correctly says to keep it.
blocking_gap: Direct network access to the origin, or any non-JS-executing fetch path to it. Any ONE of these settles it: (1) `curl -sA "GPTBot" https://www.123greetings.com/birthday/happy_birthday/endless_blessing_birthday_card.html > card.html`, then word-count the tag-stripped body (script/style removed) and `grep -oE '<video|<img|poster=|application/ld\+json|Load_Video_Card'` it — run from any unblocked machine; (2) the same URL through any server-side fetch proxy that does not execute JS (api.allorigins.win/get, r.jina.ai with `x-respond-with: html`) — both are egress-blocked here but work anywhere else; (3) Google Rich Results Test at https://search.google.com/test/rich-results on that URL, whose "View tested page > HTML" pane shows the fetched source and whose parse reveals whether the Product+VideoObject JSON-LD exists and validates; (4) Chrome DevTools "View page source" (not Inspect — source, not DOM) with JavaScript disabled. Also unverified for the same reason and settled by the same fetch: whether `Load_Video_Card()` exists, whether comments and the Latest/Related tabs are JS-loaded, and whether the JSON-LD contentUrl/embedUrl is referenced anywhere in the static markup. Prevalence across the card corpus needs a crawl of a URL sample, which no tool available here can do.

discriminating_test: The finding's observation (two similarly-named companies exist and get conflated) is cheap to check. Its load-bearing INFERENCE is causal and quantitative: that the billing-complaint corpus attributed to 123Greetings is "largely" about 123cards.com. The rival explanation that must be excluded is the obvious one: that 123Greetings itself sells a paid/subscription product, making those complaints legitimately its own. So the discriminating test has two halves: (1) Does 123cards.com actually operate a trial-to-auto-billing subscription, and does 123Greetings operate none? (2) Do the specific price points quoted in the complaint corpus ($39/yr, $2.49/mo, $29.88, 7-day trial, $49) match 123cards' published terms rather than 123Greetings'? Half (2) is the one that separates "misattributed" from "correctly attributed" — pricing fingerprints identify the biller.
test_run: Ran 6 calls. WebFetch was EGRESS_BLOCKED on every complaint host — trustpilot.com, complaintsboard.com, 123greetings.pissedconsumer.com — and on 123cards.com itself, so I could not read a single complaint body or the vendor's own pricing page directly. I therefore worked entirely from the search index. (a) Searched 123cards.com's help center: retrieved its Membership & subscriptions pages, which establish a 3-day free trial that auto-charges "for the first year of your membership" and auto-renews annually until cancelled. (b) Searched help.123greetings.com: retrieved the "Is this Service Free?" page confirming the ecard service is sponsor/ad-supported with no charge and no credit card. (c) Tested the pricing fingerprint: $2.49/mo x 12 = $29.88 exactly, so I searched that price point — it returned BirthdayAlarm, whose advertised plan is $2.49/month billed annually (~$29.99/yr with a 30-day trial), NOT 123cards. (d) Ran a brand-confusion probe naming only "123greetings" plus billing language; the result set mixed 123Greetings and 123Cards ComplaintsBoard/PissedConsumer pages together. (e) Searched for any 123Greetings paid tier; the only paid item surfaced was an uncited claim of an optional ad-free mobile app at ~$5.99/year, which I could not corroborate.

LIVE DEMONSTRATION OF THE RETRIEVAL COLLAPSE: a query naming only "123greetings" plus billing-complaint language returned, in one result set, both https://www.complaintsboard.com/123greetingscom-b125287 and https://www.complaintsboard.com/123cardscom-b132830 plus https://www.complaintsboard.com/123cardscom-membership-c1202735 — and the search layer's own synthesis over those results stated: "The actual site responsible for these charges is 123Cards.com, not 123Greetings.com." The audit's own quoted complaint figures "$2.49/month" and "$29.88 - a yearly premium membership" arithmetically match BirthdayAlarm's plan structure, not 123cards' annual-only/3-day-trial structure. corrected_claim:
CONFIRMED as observation: 123cards.com is a genuinely separate company operating a trial-to-annual-auto-billing subscription (3-day trial, card charged for a full year, auto-renewing), while 123Greetings' ecard service is free and ad-supported; and AI/search retrieval observably collapses the two — a query naming only 123Greetings returns 123Cards complaint pages and produces answers about charges that are not 123Greetings' charges. The entity-disambiguation problem is real and the GEO risk is real.

NOT SUPPORTED as stated: that the 123Greetings billing-complaint corpus is "largely" or "overwhelmingly" about 123cards specifically. That is a prevalence claim and nothing I could reach measures it — every complaint host is egress-blocked, so zero individual complaints were read or attributed. Worse, the finding's own pricing fingerprints point away from a single culprit: "$2.49/month" and "$29.88/year" match BirthdayAlarm's plan structure, and the cited "7-day trial" matches neither 123cards (3 days) nor BirthdayAlarm (30 days). The honest restatement is: the complaint corpus attributed to 123Greetings is a MIXTURE of charges from multiple similarly-positioned third-party ecard billers (123cards.com and at least one other, plus an unknown residue that may be legitimate), which retrieval systems attribute to 123Greetings. Also note the finding's evidence is stale (cites 68 PissedConsumer reviews; the index now shows 172), and I could not fully exclude a small 123Greetings paid item (an uncorroborated ~$5.99/yr ad-free mobile app) — though no such item could generate the $39/$49/$29.88 complaints.
fix_assessment:
Directionally sound and mostly low-risk, but three real hazards.

(1) LEGAL/ACCURACY RISK in the disambiguation page. The fix tells 123Greetings to publish assertions about a named competitor ("123cards.com (Denmark)", that it charges). My check shows the audit's own factual basis is partly misattributed — the $2.49/$29.88 figures belong to a BirthdayAlarm-shaped plan, and the "7-day trial" matches no verified vendor. Publishing claims about another company's billing conduct on facts this shaky invites a trade-libel/defamation complaint. The page should be confined to first-party, self-verifying statements: "123Greetings.com is free and ad-supported, never asks for a credit card, and has no subscription product. We are not affiliated with any other similarly named greeting-card site." State who you are, not what the other company does.

(2) SERP COLLATERAL DAMAGE — the non-obvious one. A page built around the literal phrasings the fix recommends ("Does 123Greetings charge a subscription?", "Why was I charged after sending a free ecard?") is a brand-plus-negative-term page on the brand's own domain. It will rank for brand queries and can surface "charged"/"subscription" language in the SERP and in AI summaries for users who had no such concern, reinforcing the association it means to break. Frame the page positively and title it as an identity/affiliation page ("123Greetings is free — who we are and who we are not"), not as a billing-complaint FAQ.

(3) FAQPage schema is likely dead weight. Google narrowed FAQ rich results in August 2023 to well-known authoritative government and health sites; a consumer ecard site will almost certainly get no rich result from it. I did not re-verify this against developers.google.com in this run (budget spent on the discriminating test), so treat it as a caution to confirm before the effort is booked. The markup is still harmless for entity parsing, just not a SERP win.

No deindexation risk and no ranking-loss risk in any of the four actions. Action (2) (sameAs/alternateName on the Organization node) is unambiguously correct and is the highest value-per-effort item, since machine-separating the two entities is the actual root fix. Action (3) (on-record replies) is sound; keep replies individually worded rather than a pasted identical sentence, which review platforms flag as templated.
blocking_gap: Prevalence is the whole unverified half, and it needs the complaint bodies, all of which are egress-blocked here. The settling test: `curl -sL https://123greetings.pissedconsumer.com/review.html https://www.complaintsboard.com/123greetingscom-b125287 https://www.trustpilot.com/review/www.123greetings.com 'https://www.bbb.org/us/ny/plainview/profile/greeting-card-store/123-greetings-0121-89290'` then classify every billing complaint on three fingerprints — charged amount, trial length, and the merchant descriptor the complainant says appeared on their bank statement — against 123cards' published terms (3-day trial, annual charge) versus BirthdayAlarm's ($2.49/mo billed annually, 30-day trial) versus 123Greetings' own (none). The fraction whose descriptor or amount/trial pair matches a third party is the number the word "largely" is standing in for. The merchant descriptor is the single most decisive field: it names the actual biller and needs no inference. A secondary gap: confirming whether 123Greetings sells any paid item at all requires fetching www.123greetings.com and its app store listings, also blocked.

discriminating_test: The finding has two separable parts. (1) OBSERVATION — "the JSON-LD Organization node on 123greetings.com card pages contains name and url only, no logo/description/foundingDate/founder/address/sameAs." The only test that separates true from false is reading the raw served HTML of a card page (and an m. card page) and enumerating the properties of the Organization node, e.g. curl the page and extract every <script type="application/ld+json">, or run Google's Rich Results Test on that URL. Nothing about the index, the snippet or any third-party profile can distinguish "Organization node with 2 properties" from "Organization node with 9 properties" or "no Organization node at all" — so this part is testable ONLY with direct HTTP access. (2) INFERENCE — "without sameAs the engine cannot merge the third-party profiles into one entity, and this node is the prerequisite for any Knowledge Panel." The discriminating test here is Google's own published policy on Organization markup: whether Google states sameAs/logo/founder are required and whether Organization markup is a precondition for a knowledge panel, versus merely one input the Knowledge Graph may use.

corrected_claim:
Split it:

OBSERVATION (untested here): "The Organization JSON-LD on card pages carries name and url only." Status: neither confirmed nor refuted. It originates from a prior source review, not from anything reproducible in this environment. It should be re-flagged as needs_live_fetch: true — the finding currently carries needs_live_fetch: false, which is wrong for a claim about the contents of a served script tag.

PREMISE (confirmed): the third-party facts about this entity genuinely conflict — CB Insights says Mumbai, Crunchbase/ZoomInfo/TheOrg say 1674 Broadway, New York. So the "conflicting third-party facts" the finding is built on are real and independently attested.

INFERENCE (overstated as written, in two specific places):
1. "Without sameAs there is nothing linking the site to its Crunchbase/LinkedIn/Trustpilot/Play/App Store identities, so the engine cannot merge those into one entity." Not supported. Google documents sameAs as something it "can make general use of," not as the reconciliation mechanism; entity merging also runs on outbound/inbound links, co-citation, name+address matching and third-party feeds. The defensible version: "sameAs is the cheapest explicit disambiguation signal the brand controls, and absent it the merge depends entirely on signals the brand does not control."
2. "This node is also the prerequisite for any Knowledge Panel." Refuted as stated. Google's wording is that additional organizational details "can make markup eligible for knowledge panels" and can influence "which logo is shown in Search results and your knowledge panel" — eligibility and presentation, not a precondition for the panel existing. Knowledge panels are generated from the Knowledge Graph and routinely exist for sites with no Organization markup.

Also correct: "There are no required properties for Organization structured data" — so the finding's framing of a 2-property node as a spec violation is wrong; it is a thin-but-valid node, which is an opportunity-cost problem, not a compliance problem.
fix_assessment:
The fix is directionally sound and Google-endorsed in shape (Google explicitly recommends adding as many relevant properties as possible, and names logo, name/alternateName, url, address, telephone), effort genuinely small, and no deindexation or ranking-loss risk: adding properties to an Organization node cannot demote pages. Three concrete cautions.

1. THE ADDRESS LINE IS THE DANGEROUS ONE. The fix says "address (the one canonical HQ)" as though a canonical HQ is known. It is not — that is the very conflict the finding cites (New York per Crunchbase/ZoomInfo/TheOrg vs Mumbai per CB Insights). Emitting a PostalAddress picked from an aggregator turns an unresolved fact into a first-party machine-readable assertion, and if wrong it will propagate and become harder to correct than the current silence. The address value must come from the company's own registration/pressroom (info.123greetings.com pressroom exists), not from this audit, and if the company operates both a US entity and an India office the markup should say which one it is asserting.

2. FOUNDER VALUES ARE HALF-CHECKED. "founder [Arvind Kajaria, Sharad Kajaria]" is attested but the roles are not identical across sources (Arvind: "Co Founder & Managing Partner"/"Founder & CEO"; Sharad: President 1997–2011, currently CEO/founder of a different company, 123Stores). Asserting both as schema:founder is probably correct but needs a first-party source, and each should carry a sameAs to the specific person profile rather than a bare name string, or it adds two more unreconcilable name-only nodes.

3. THE sameAs URLs THEMSELVES CHECK OUT. crunchbase.com/organization/123greetings, com.g123 on Play and id718873921 on the App Store are all real and all belong to this brand — the fix is not sending engines to wrong profiles. The Wikidata clause is conditional ("once created") and safe. One unverified mechanical caution I could not test because developers.google.com is blocked to direct fetch: Google's guidance is oriented to a single Organization node on the most representative page, so the "emit sitewide on card, hub, tag, m. and homepage templates" instruction should be implemented strictly as the fix says — one canonical node, referenced by @id — and not as N duplicated full Organization blocks, which risks conflicting nodes if any template drifts.

Sequencing note: this fix asserts facts. Running it before founding-year-conflict, hq-location-conflict and card-count-conflict are resolved just hard-codes whichever version the implementer happened to pick.

discriminating_test: The finding bundles an observation (third-party copy criticizes 123Greetings for ads, in reproducible language) with a causal claim (ad experience is THE blocker on AI citation, and no other work will move sentiment while it persists). These need different tests. (1) OBSERVATION: do the exact quoted strings actually exist in the indexed corpus? Test = site-agnostic WebSearch on the verbatim phrases; a snippet hit proves the string is in the index. (2) INFERENCE: the test must discriminate "ads are the decisive cause" from three rival explanations — (a) the criticism is competitor-authored comparison copy, not independent editorial; (b) ads are inseparably bundled with "dated designs" and "no personalization," which the fix does not address and which are the roundups' actual stated ranking criteria; (c) a separate and louder negative corpus (billing/unauthorized charges/undelivered cards) exists that the fix does not touch. corrected_claim: Ad saturation and dated design are a real, reproducible and widely-indexed criticism of 123greetings.com, and the recipient-side sentence the finding flags ("the ads show to both you and the person opening the card") exists verbatim in 2026 comparison copy. But the stated cause is overreached on four counts. The criticism is not carried by "independent publishers": the two 2026 roundups cited are published by RecoCards and Heartdrop, both competing ecard vendors that rank their own product first. The roundups do not exclude 123Greetings — they list it and recommend it for the free-basic slot ("works in a pinch"), demoting it on personalization and AI features, criteria the ad fix does not touch. The ad complaint travels inseparably with "dated designs" and "no personalization" in the very sentences quoted, so removing ads leaves two-thirds of each sentence intact. And a separate, louder negative corpus — unauthorized billing, $49 charges after free trials, undelivered cards, unreachable support, PissedConsumer 1.6/5 — is at least as plausible a driver of model reluctance and is untouched by the fix. The assertion that "no schema, sitemap or content work will move AI sentiment while this sentence keeps being written" is unsupported and is contradicted by the site already shipping and publicizing an ad-free recipient experience (Pro, $5.99/yr) without the copy changing. Severity: real UX problem worth fixing on its merits, not the single gating mechanism for AI citation.
fix_assessment: First half (strip interstitial/anchor/side-rail units from the card-view and /do/viewecard templates) is sound on UX merit and carries low SEO risk — recipient card-view URLs are transactional, per-recipient, thin pages that carry little organic ranking value, and cutting interstitials also reduces Core Web Vitals and Better Ads Standards exposure. No deindexation risk. But the finding does not price it, and the revenue collateral is material and specific: the recipient view is plausibly a large share of total ad impressions (every sent card generates a view), and the company's own public position is "ads are what make that possible." More sharply, 123Greetings Pro at $5.99/yr sells precisely this — "the only ecard subscription where ad-free means no interruptions for the sender and the person receiving it." Making the recipient view ad-free for everyone cannibalizes the one differentiated benefit of the paid tier. That tradeoff needs a decision, not an assumption. Second half (take the dated blog post and FAQ note to the publishers in pr-target-list to get their copy updated) is unlikely to work as specified: the named publishers are direct competitors whose roundups exist to rank their own products first, so they have a commercial incentive not to upgrade a rival's entry. No collateral damage, but low expected yield — this is the weakest part of the fix. Recommend two redirects: (a) point outreach at genuinely independent surfaces (Wikipedia/Wikidata, app-store listing copy, Reddit threads) rather than competitor roundups; (b) spend the reclaimed effort on the billing/unauthorized-charge and undelivered-card complaint corpus, which is louder, more damaging to trust signals, and currently unaddressed by any finding in this audit.
blocking_gap: Two sub-claims remain untestable here. (1) The finding's technical basis — "four concurrent ad stacks (GPT with 13 slots including interstitial and anchor, AdSense auto ads, AdPushup, Taboola, with interstitial unhideWindow active)" — depends on the live DOM of an egress-blocked host. If descriptive occasion-nested card-detail URLs exist and are what Google surfaces for a card-level query, the competitive-gap claim is refuted and only a duplicate-route problem remains. fix_assessment:
The proposed fix is unsound as written and should not ship in its current form.

1. It builds a THIRD card-URL template. The site already has /{occasion}/{subcategory}/{slug}.html as the descriptive canonical. Adding /do/card/<id>/<slug> and 301-ing the bare ID into it entrenches a parallel card-URL space rather than collapsing it, worsening the duplication it is meant to cure. The "longer term, mirror the AG pattern with the occasion prefix" step is effectively asking to build what already exists.

2. Wrong direction of redirect. If the bare-ID route is to be 301'd anywhere, the defensible target is the existing descriptive .html canonical for that card — which requires an id→canonical-URL map the team already has internally. That is a smaller change than the proposed new route and resolves the duplication.

3. Real collateral-damage risk: /do/card/<id> is very plausibly the link embedded in delivered e-card notification emails and shares, and /do/viewecard is a live adjacent route. Blanket-301-ing 30k bare-ID URLs without first confirming which are recipient-delivery endpoints risks breaking the product's core delivery flow. Any such change needs the delivery path audited first.

4. "Large" effort is misallocated if the premise is the competitive URL gap, since that gap is not real. The title-template failure on /do/card/ (generic homepage title) is independently confirmed here and is the part worth fixing — and it is cheap relative to a route migration.

URLs sharing one generic title is consistent with the latter.

Real collateral risks: (1) A whole-host 301 migration of an indexed URL space causes months of ranking volatility; the m. URLs shown above are indexed and currently earn traffic, so this needs a 1:1 path map — m.123greetings.com/do/cards/birth_bronsis/p/2 to its exact www equivalent, never a blanket redirect to the www homepage, which is the classic way these migrations lose the rankings they were meant to consolidate. (2) The m. 301s must stay live permanently, not for a release cycle. (3) Do not remove rel=alternate/rel=canonical pairing before the redirects are in place; stripping the annotation while both hosts still serve content turns an annotated duplicate pair into an unannotated one, which is worse than the status quo. (4) The interim advice (absolute bidirectional https alternate/canonical, m. templates rendering the same title/description/JSON-LD as www) is low-risk and correct per Google's stated pairing rule, and is the part that can ship now. (5) "Put a decision in front of leadership" is a process step, not a fix — the finding should not be counted as remediable by writing a memo, and its "critical" severity is better read as strategic scope than as urgency.

discriminating_test: The finding has two separable parts. OBSERVATION: competitors publish "best ecard site" roundups and 123greetings publishes none. INFERENCE (the load-bearing part): those vendor-owned roundups are what answer engines actually retrieve for category comparison queries, so a competitor's framing becomes the cited passage. The discriminating test for the inference is NOT to re-observe that the roundups exist — it is to run the actual commercial-investigation query an answer engine would serve and inspect the resulting retrieval set: if it is populated by vendor-owned roundups with zero 123greetings comparison pages, AND the synthesized answer's characterization of 123greetings traces to competitor-authored text, the mechanic is demonstrated rather than merely asserted. Rival explanations this discriminates against: (a) the roundups exist but are outranked by neutral third-party publishers, so vendor framing does not dominate retrieval; (b) 123greetings already supplies the cited passage from its own www pages.

(3) WebSearch "site:123greetings.com best free ecard sites comparison alternatives" — absence probe on the main domain with comparison vocabulary. (4) WebSearch "free ecard sites no sign up best" — a second, independent commercial-investigation query to test whether the pattern generalizes beyond one head term. corrected_claim: Substantially accurate; three precisifications. (1) "123greetings currently contributes none of the text that gets cited" overstates slightly — its homepage does enter the retrieval set for some category queries and its brand copy ("no sign-up required", event reminders, address book) appears to reach the synthesized answer. The precise claim is that 123greetings contributes none of the COMPARISON text: it has no page that participates in the ranked-list genre where the category's framing is set. (2) "written by parties with an interest in ranking 123greetings second" — the self-interest is confirmed (vendors demonstrably lead with themselves), but the specific ordinal position of 123greetings inside any roundup is UNVERIFIED, because every roundup body is egress-blocked. Drop the "second" specificity. Notably, where 123greetings is described it is described favorably ("cheapest", "no sign-up") — the harm is loss of framing control, not active disparagement. (3) "every comparison query in the category" is extrapolation from n=2 queries; both confirmed, but WebSearch returns ~10 US results with no rank positions and no counts, so this establishes the pattern on head terms, not across the full query set.
fix_assessment: Directionally sound and low-risk: this is net-new content on a subdomain, so there is no deindexation or ranking-loss exposure — nothing existing is being changed or consolidated. Three caveats. (1) STALE SUB-RECOMMENDATION: "Mark up each with ItemList + FAQPage" is partly obsolete. Google restricted FAQ rich results to well-known government and health sites in August 2023 and then removed them entirely on 7 May 2026; the search appearance, the rich-results report and Rich Results Test support are being dropped through June–August 2026. FAQPage remains a valid schema.org type and may still be parsed by non-Google retrieval systems, so including it is harmless — but it will deliver zero SERP feature and should not be budgeted as if it will. ItemList is unaffected and remains the right markup for a ranked list. (2) SELF-PREFERENCE RISK: the fix asks 123greetings to publish roundups naming competitors, i.e. to do what the competitors do. A vendor-authored comparison that places itself first without genuine stated criteria and honest drawbacks is exactly the self-serving-review pattern Google's site-reputation and spam guidance targets. The fix's own instruction to include "explicit criteria, named competitors including paid ones" mitigates this, but it must be enforced, including real limitations of 123greetings itself (ads on the free tier, dated UI), or the pages risk being discounted rather than cited. (3) COMPETITIVE REALITY: 123greetings enters this genre late against incumbents with accumulated link equity and 2026-dated pages; the "large" effort rating is honest, and expected time-to-effect is quarters, not weeks. Recommend prioritizing the two queries I verified as vendor-dominated ("best ecard sites", "free ecard sites no sign up") over the speculative long-tail titles in the list.
blocking_gap: Two residual gaps, neither of which changes the verdict. (1) Ordinal positions inside the roundups could not be checked — every competitor domain (sendwishonline.com, www.kudoboard.com, recocards.com) returned EGRESS_BLOCKED, contrary to the task brief that said competitor sites are fetchable. Settled by: curl -sL "https://sendwishonline.com/en/articles/best-sites-for-ecards" | grep -i -A5 "123greetings" — or the same against recocards.com/blog/ecards/best-ecard-websites/. (2) Prevalence across the full comparison-query set is unestablished; WebSearch is US-only, ~10 results, no rank positions, no counts. Settled by a rank-tracking tool (Semrush/Ahrefs keyword-by-URL export) over the category's commercial-investigation keyword list, or by Search Console impression data for 123greetings on those terms.
